$comment: Describes this codebase, so it ships with the frontend rather than coming from the API — see docs/adr/0005-engineering-section.md. Placeholders like {tests} are filled from content/engineering-facts.json, which is generated from the repository. Never write a number here by hand.
title: How this site is built
lead: This portfolio is a working system, not a styled CV. It has a frontend, an API and a database because the point was to walk the whole path — data model, application layer, HTTP contract, client, deployment — and be able to explain every decision along it.

why.title: Why a frontend, an API and a database
paragraphs: A personal portfolio does not need a database. Ten static pages would have loaded faster and cost nothing to run. That is precisely why building it that way would have said nothing about the work I actually do.

So the content lives in PostgreSQL, is served by an ASP.NET Core API with a real contract, and is consumed by an Angular frontend that prerenders to static files. Every layer is small on purpose — the goal was a complete flow that holds together, not a large system that impresses by size.

The constraint I set myself was the one that is easy to break: no layer, pattern or dependency exists unless I can say what problem it solves and what it costs. Where I chose not to add something, that is written down too.

focus.title: Where the weight sits
paragraphs: I work on backend. The site reflects that honestly rather than hiding it: the depth is in the domain model, the bilingual content design, the API contract and the infrastructure. The frontend is careful and deliberately plain — it is the window, not the exhibit.

The parts I would actually want to be asked about are here: a business rule that is subtle enough to get wrong, a translation model that survives a third language, one seam that let storage change without the contract moving, and a check that caught two implementations quietly disagreeing.

architecture.title: Architecture
architecture.description: Angular prerenders every route and locale to static HTML at build time, served by nginx. The API is stateless and read-only. PostgreSQL holds the content, seeded from reviewed files in the repository.
notes: The frontend ships a build-time snapshot of the content. If the API is unreachable or cold-starting, the page still renders — it shows cached content rather than a spinner or an error.
That is not decoration. A portfolio that shows an error while someone is looking at it during an interview has failed at the only moment that mattered.

decisions.title: Bilingual content, English default
decisions.problem: Two audiences that do not overlap: international recruiters and the Colombian market. Serving one halves the reach.
decisions.decision: English at /en, Spanish at /es with full parity. UI strings switch at runtime; content is translated per locale in the database.
decisions.rejected: Auto-redirecting by Accept-Language, which would destabilise the canonical URLs prerendering depends on and take control away from the reader.
decisions.cost: Every content change is two changes, and prerendering doubles the generated routes.

decisions.title: Prerendered, not a single-page app
decisions.problem: A plain SPA returns an empty document to crawlers and to the link-preview bots used by LinkedIn and WhatsApp — exactly the channels a portfolio travels through.
decisions.decision: Angular with prerendering. Every route and locale becomes static HTML, served by nginx with no Node process in production.
decisions.rejected: Server-side rendering on every request, for content that changes a handful of times a year.
decisions.cost: Content edits need a rebuild, and build time grows with routes times locales.

decisions.title: Years of experience are computed, never stored
decisions.problem: Two roles held at the same time are not double the experience, and a career gap is not experience at all. A number typed into a file goes stale the month after it is written.
decisions.decision: The domain unions the months every role covers and divides by twelve. The same rule drives the site and the generated CV, so the two cannot disagree.
decisions.rejected: Summing role durations, which inflates any overlap; and measuring first start to last end, which counts gaps as experience.
decisions.cost: A subtle rule needs tests that state the intent, including one pinned to the real career.

decisions.title: One seam between the application and its storage
decisions.problem: The content started as files and had to become PostgreSQL without the API contract moving.
decisions.decision: A single interface returning the whole resolved content for one language. Both a file source and a database source implement it; which one runs is configuration.
decisions.rejected: A repository per entity, and a generic repository wrapped around Entity Framework — patterns with nothing to do here.
decisions.cost: Two implementations of one contract, which is why the parity check below exists.

decisions.title: Translations as rows, resolved at seed time
decisions.problem: Storing translated text in columns makes a third language a schema migration. Storing it sparsely makes every read do fallback logic.
decisions.decision: Base tables hold the facts; translation tables are keyed by entity and language code, and are written already resolved — one complete row per language.
decisions.rejected: Per-language columns, and field-level fallback at read time.
decisions.cost: The seed does more work so that reads do less, and the resolution logic must exist in exactly one place.

decisions.title: No dependency that earns nothing
decisions.problem: It is easy to add a well-known library because it looks professional rather than because it is needed.
decisions.decision: Structured JSON logging with what the framework already provides, since every container platform collects stdout.
decisions.rejected: A third-party logging library that would have produced the same lines.
decisions.cost: Slightly more setup by hand, and a name a reviewer might expect to see and not find.

flows.title: How a request resolves its language
flows.description: Explicit parameter, then the Accept-Language header honouring quality values and reducing regional tags, then English. Every response reports which language it resolved and from where, so a caller never has to guess. A malformed header falls back rather than failing — a broken header from some client is not a reason to refuse a public page.

flows.title: How content reaches the page
flows.description: Reviewed files in the repository are the source of truth. A seeder loads them into PostgreSQL, recording a fingerprint so a deploy that changed nothing rewrites nothing. The API reads from there. The frontend prerenders against the API at build time and revalidates at runtime, falling back to what it prerendered.

flows.title: The CV is generated from the same content
flows.description: The CV is not a hand-edited file kept alongside the site — it is built from the same reviewed content, in both languages, and fits two pages by measuring the rendered output rather than by guessing a font size. A correction is made once.

dataModel.title: Data model
dataModel.description: {tables} tables. Facts live on the base tables; translated text lives in translation tables keyed by entity and language, which makes a third language a data change rather than a migration.
notes: Check constraints refuse a period that ends before it starts and a month outside 1–12, because a negative duration would render as nonsense on a public page.
Projects reference roles with a restricted delete rather than a cascade: removing a role that still has projects is a mistake worth surfacing, not a silent loss of content.

testing.title: Testing
testing.description: {tests} tests — {backendTests} on the backend, {frontendTests} on the frontend — covering the parts where being wrong would be invisible rather than obvious.
items: The tenure rule: overlapping roles, a role inside another, a career gap, and one test pinned to the real career so the site and the CV cannot drift apart.

The HTTP contract through the real pipeline against the real content — language negotiation, the problem-document shape, correlation ids that are sanitised before they reach a log, and an assertion that no response ever contains a phone number.
The database path against a real PostgreSQL in a container: the migration, the check constraints that refuse an impossible period, and the fact that reseeding unchanged content changes nothing.

A parity check comparing the file source and the database source across both languages, as a script and as a test. It found a real disagreement about ordering that no unit test would have caught, which is the reason it exists.

The frontend: the URL-to-locale wiring, the rendered links of the language switcher, and the fallback to the embedded snapshot when the API is unreachable or answers with something that is not content.

operations.title: Operations
items: Liveness runs no checks at all — it answers whether the process is wedged. A content problem must not make an orchestrator restart a healthy process.
Readiness loads the content in every supported language, which catches the case where English works and Spanish does not — a failure that would otherwise only be seen by Spanish-speaking visitors.
Every request carries a correlation id, accepted from the caller when well-formed and generated otherwise, echoed back and attached to the logs.
Errors are RFC 7807 problem documents from one handler. Only exceptions the application defines contribute their message; anything unexpected stays generic.
No phone number is published, and the CV in the repository is the redacted one. The personal number lives in an untracked file the build reads if it is there.
